subject: biology

items.q: A survey of an island records three findings: the island contains six distinct ecosystems; 420 species have been identified; and its population of one lizard species carries 18 alleles at a studied gene, compared with 4 alleles in the same species on a neighbouring island. Which of these findings describe the island's biodiversity?
items.correct: All three of the findings, because biodiversity includes ecosystem, species and genetic diversity
items.misconception: Only the count of 420 species, because biodiversity means the variety of species
items.why: GCSE and MYP courses define biodiversity as 'the variety of all the different species of organisms', and diversity indices in earlier fieldwork are calculated from species counts, so the species level becomes the whole meaning of the word. Species diversity is one level of biodiversity. Biodiversity is the variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations: the range of ecosystems, the species within them and their relative abundance, and the variety of alleles within each species. Counting species alone misses the other two levels.
items.specStatementText: Biodiversity is variety at three levels
items.random_wrong: The six ecosystems and 420 species, but not the alleles, which are variation within a species

items.q: Cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus) show extremely little genetic variation: unrelated cheetahs are so alike that skin grafts between them are not rejected. In a reserve, cheetah numbers have been stable for 20 years, and the species present and their relative abundances have not changed. Which statement about biodiversity in the reserve is correct?
items.correct: The cheetah's genetic diversity is low, although the reserve's species diversity is unchanged
items.misconception: The cheetahs' uniformity does not affect biodiversity, because the number of species present is unchanged
items.why: Diversity is introduced as a contrast between kinds of organism, and genetic variation is taught separately under inheritance and evolution, so students file the two ideas in different places and do not connect them. Genetic diversity is a level of biodiversity in its own right. A species whose populations have lost alleles has lost biodiversity even if the species itself survives, and it has less capacity to adapt to change, which is why conservation programmes try to maintain genetic diversity, not just species numbers.
items.specStatementText: Biodiversity is variety at three levels
items.random_wrong: Species diversity is low, because all the cheetahs are genetically almost identical

items.q: Two taxonomists study the same collection of ground beetles. One recognizes 12 species. The other recognizes 4 species, treating the small differences in colour and size that separate the other taxonomist's species as variation within a species. Which statement about this situation is correct?
items.correct: The first taxonomist is a splitter and the second a lumper; both are valid classifications
items.misconception: Only one of the counts can be valid, because the number of species in the collection is an objective fact
items.why: Classification is taught as a settled hierarchy of named groups, and species counts are printed as precise figures, so students see them as measured facts rather than as the outcome of decisions about how much difference counts. Deciding how much difference separates two species is a judgement. A splitter treats small, consistent differences as separate species; a lumper treats them as variation within one species. Both are valid classifications of the same observations, which is why species counts differ between sources (NOS).
items.specStatementText: More species now than ever, and most are still undescribed
items.random_wrong: The 12-species count shows that the collection holds three times the biodiversity found by the other taxonomist

items.q: Polynesian settlers reached New Zealand around 1300 CE. Within about two centuries the North Island giant moa (Dinornis novaezealandiae), a flightless bird that had evolved with no mammalian predators, matured slowly and laid few eggs, was extinct. Archaeological sites contain large numbers of butchered moa bones and moa eggshell. Which explanation of the extinction is best supported?
items.correct: Hunting of adults and taking of eggs, with burning of forest, removed moa faster than a slow-breeding population could replace them
items.misconception: A natural shift in climate at the time, of the kind behind earlier mass extinctions, removed the moa independently of the settlers
items.why: Students learn about earlier mass extinctions with dramatic natural causes, and hear that 'most species that ever lived are extinct', so extinction feels like something that just happens rather than something people do. Background extinction is natural, but the present rate is far above it, and every well-documented recent extinction traces to human activity: hunting and over-exploitation, habitat destruction, pollution and introduced species. The moa disappeared within two centuries of human settlement; the monk seal was hunted for oil.
items.specStatementText: Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
items.random_wrong: Rats and dogs brought by the settlers ate the eggs, since a few thousand people with stone tools could not hunt out so big a bird

items.q: Which statement about the Caribbean monk seal (Neomonachus tropicalis) case study is correct?
items.correct: It was hunted for the oil in its blubber from the 1490s, an anthropogenic extinction of a marine mammal species
items.misconception: It became extinct only after industrial fishing fleets reached the Caribbean in the twentieth century
items.why: Media coverage of biodiversity loss shows chainsaws, trawlers and cities, so students link extinction with industrial scale and assume earlier societies lived in balance with nature. Extinction depends on the balance between removal and replacement. Moa matured slowly, laid few eggs and had no fear of predators, so hunting of adults and eggs by a small population, with burning of forest, removed them faster than they could breed. Caribbean monk seal hunting began in the 1490s, long before industrial fishing.
items.specStatementText: Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
items.random_wrong: It shows that marine species are otherwise safe, since the open ocean is too large for people to affect them

items.q: Mixed dipterocarp forest once covered the lowlands of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula. Which description of how this ecosystem has been lost is correct?
items.correct: Logging for hardwood timber, followed by clearance and burning of the land for oil palm and pulpwood plantations
items.misconception: Conversion to oil palm has replaced one kind of forest with another, so species have been lost but the ecosystem has not
items.why: In everyday language any area of trees is a forest, and satellite measures of 'tree cover' or 'forest area' used in the news count plantations as forest, so the ecosystem and the crop look the same on a map. An ecosystem is a community interacting with its environment. Mixed dipterocarp forest holds hundreds of tree species with their associated animals, fungi and processes; an oil palm plantation supports a small fraction of them. Ecosystem loss occurs when the characteristic community disappears, whether or not trees remain.
items.specStatementText: Whole ecosystems are being lost to human activity
items.random_wrong: Droughts and forest fires that are unconnected with human activity have destroyed most of the lowland forest

items.q: A survey of a lowland region of Borneo reports the following percentages of the land area. Tree canopy cover above 60%: 82% in 1990, 74% in 2020. Mixed dipterocarp forest: 80% in 1990, 31% in 2020. Oil palm and pulpwood plantation: 1% in 1990, 42% in 2020. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
items.correct: Canopy cover understates the loss, because plantations keep tree cover but are not the forest ecosystem
items.misconception: The forest was lost mainly to drought and fire, which are natural events and so do not count as anthropogenic ecosystem loss
items.why: Images of ecosystem loss show bulldozers and chainsaws, and fire and drought are familiar as weather, so students separate intentional clearance from everything that seems to happen on its own. The guide includes causes that are directly or indirectly anthropogenic. Intact dipterocarp forest rarely burns; fire spreads through logged forest and drained peatland during droughts, and fires are often started to clear land. Climate change driven by human activity makes such droughts more frequent, so these losses trace back to human activity.
items.specStatementText: Whole ecosystems are being lost to human activity
items.random_wrong: Little ecosystem loss has occurred, because canopy cover fell by only 8 percentage points and most of the region still carries trees

items.q: A woodland was surveyed for ground beetles in 2000 and again in 2020 using the same pitfall-trap method and the same trapping effort. In 2000, 8 species were caught and the most abundant species made up 20% of the individuals. In 2020, 8 species were caught and the most abundant species made up 75% of the individuals. What do these results show?
items.correct: Species richness was unchanged but species evenness fell, a change that only a repeated survey could reveal
items.misconception: Biodiversity was unchanged, because both surveys recorded the same number of beetle species
items.why: Counting species is the simplest fieldwork measure, and earlier courses compare habitats by number of species found, so richness stands in for diversity and relative abundance is not considered. Species diversity has two components: richness (how many species) and evenness (how evenly individuals are spread among them). A community in which one species has risen from 20% to 75% of individuals has lost diversity even though every species is still present; repeated surveys are needed to detect both kinds of change.
items.specStatementText: Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
items.random_wrong: The 2020 survey alone would have shown the decline, since it recorded the dominance of one species

items.q: A national scheme asks members of the public to record every bird species seen in their garden during one hour on a chosen weekend each year. Over 10 years, the number of records of a rare species rose from 40 to 300, while the number of participants rose from 5 000 to 60 000. Which statement about this evidence is correct?
items.correct: Records per participant fell from 0.008 to 0.005, so the rise in records reflects effort, not evidence of an increase
items.misconception: The species has become about seven times more common over the ten years, because its records rose from 40 to 300 sightings
items.why: Recording apps and national counts present headline totals, and students are used to survey results being reported without a measure of effort, so a rise in records reads as a rise in the species. Citizen science brings benefits, giving coverage that scientists alone could not achieve, but also unique methodological concerns: participant numbers change from year to year, identification skill varies, and sites are chosen rather than sampled at random. Records must be expressed per unit of effort and checked before they count as evidence (NOS).
items.specStatementText: Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
items.random_wrong: The results became verifiable evidence as soon as the scheme published its yearly totals on its website

items.q: Why do surveys of biodiversity need to be repeated to provide evidence for a biodiversity crisis?
items.correct: A change in species richness or evenness can only be shown by comparing surveys made at two different times
items.misconception: A single thorough survey is sufficient, provided that it covers a wide enough range of habitats around the world
items.why: Fieldwork at GCSE and MYP usually involves one sampling exercise whose results are interpreted on their own, so students are used to drawing conclusions from a single snapshot. A single survey measures the state of a community at one time. Evidence of change requires the survey to be repeated, using the same methods and effort, so that richness and evenness at different times can be compared; this is why long-running monitoring schemes are so valuable.
items.specStatementText: Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
items.random_wrong: Repeating a survey is needed only when the first survey was carried out by citizen scientists rather than experts

items.q: Which factor is the overarching cause of the current biodiversity crisis, driving each of the specific causes?
items.correct: Growth of the human population
items.misconception: Spread of cities over natural habitat
items.why: Population growth is pictured as more houses and bigger cities, because that is the visible effect, and each specific cause is taught with its own examples, so students do not see population growth as lying behind all of them. Urbanization is one specific cause, but the land taken by cities is small compared with the land cleared to feed and supply their inhabitants. Population growth is overarching because it multiplies the demand for food, timber, fish, energy and traded goods that drives every specific cause.
items.specStatementText: What is driving the crisis

items.q: The zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha), native to the Caspian and Black Sea region, was first recorded in the North American Great Lakes in 1988, having arrived in the ballast water of ships. It has since spread widely and smothers native mussels. Which statement correctly relates this case to the causes of the biodiversity crisis?
items.correct: It is an invasive alien species whose spread is a consequence of global transport, one of the specific causes of the crisis
items.misconception: It reached the Great Lakes by natural range expansion, so its spread is not a human cause of biodiversity loss
items.why: The word 'invasive' makes the species sound like the active agent, and students learn about natural dispersal and migration, so the human transport step is left out of the story. An alien species is one that people have carried outside its natural range, and it becomes invasive when it establishes and harms native species. The guide lists the spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species due to global transport as a specific cause of the biodiversity crisis.
items.specStatementText: What is driving the crisis
items.random_wrong: Its spread results from urbanization along the lake shores, the route by which population growth affects biodiversity

items.q: Seeds of many tropical rainforest trees are killed by the drying and freezing used in seed banks. A conservation programme wants to conserve one such tree species, whose natural forest is being logged. Which approach to conserving this species is appropriate?
items.correct: Store its germ plasm as cultured tissue in a tissue bank, alongside protection of the remaining forest in situ
items.misconception: Dry and freeze its seeds in a seed bank, because seed banks can preserve the germ plasm of any species of plant
items.why: The seeds students handle, such as beans and cereals, survive years of dry storage, and the Svalbard and Millennium seed banks are presented as stores for all the world's plants, so seed banking seems universal. Seeds that tolerate drying and freezing can be banked for decades. Seeds that do not are conserved in tissue banks, as cultured tissue or frozen cells, or as living collections in botanic gardens. This is one reason why different species require different measures.
items.specStatementText: No single conservation method is enough
items.random_wrong: Grow the tree in a botanic garden alone, so that its natural forest habitat no longer needs to be protected

items.q: Which description of an approach to the conservation of biodiversity is correct?
items.correct: Rewilding restores natural processes to an area, often by reintroducing missing species
items.misconception: Nature reserves conserve species by keeping people out, so no management is needed
items.why: Reserves are described as 'protected areas', and students learn that human activity is the cause of the crisis, so removing humans seems to be the whole solution. Many ecosystems are shaped by processes that people now have to maintain or replace, and threats such as invasive species, pollution and fragmentation cross reserve boundaries. Management of nature reserves is listed in the guide as an approach in its own right, and rewilding is a deliberate attempt to restore the natural processes that make self-sustaining ecosystems possible.
items.specStatementText: No single conservation method is enough
items.random_wrong: Ex situ conservation in zoos can, by itself, secure the future of an endangered animal species

items.q: The EDGE of Existence programme scores species for Evolutionary Distinctiveness (ED) and Global Endangerment (GE). Four species are assessed: W has high ED and is Critically Endangered; X has high ED and is of Least Concern; Y has low ED and is Critically Endangered; Z has low ED and is of Least Concern. Which species does the EDGE programme prioritize, and why?
items.correct: Species W, because it combines few close relatives with a high risk of extinction
items.misconception: Species Y, because the most endangered species must be conserved first, whatever its relatives
items.why: The IUCN Red List and charity campaigns rank species by threat and by appeal, and pandas, tigers and whales dominate conservation publicity, so threat and charisma become the only criteria students know. Threat is one criterion. EDGE adds evolutionary distinctiveness so that species with few close living relatives, which represent branches of the tree of life found nowhere else, are not lost while attention goes to well-known species with many relatives.
items.specStatementText: EDGE prioritizes species that are distinct and endangered
items.random_wrong: Species X, because the most distinct lineage is the oldest and should be conserved first

items.q: A conservation budget can fund a recovery programme for only one of two species: a large, well-known mammal with many close relatives that attracts tourists, or a small, little-known amphibian with no close living relatives that is Critically Endangered. Which statement about deciding between them is correct?
items.correct: The EDGE rationale favours the amphibian, but the choice also has ethical, economic and cultural implications that need to be debated
items.misconception: The decision is purely scientific: the species' scores settle the matter, so there is nothing left to debate
items.why: Students learn that science gives objective answers, and EDGE presents its priorities as numbers, so a ranked list looks like a decision rather than one input to it. EDGE scores identify species whose loss would remove the most unique evolutionary history, but choosing where to spend limited money also involves people's livelihoods, cultural values, politics and ethics. The guide's NOS point is that such issues need to be debated (NOS).
items.specStatementText: EDGE prioritizes species that are distinct and endangered
items.random_wrong: The mammal must be chosen, because conservation effort should go to the species that people care about most

items.q: Is the variety of ecosystems in a region part of its biodiversity?
items.correct: Yes. Ecosystem diversity, the range of ecosystems present, is one of the three levels of biodiversity.
items.misconception: Biodiversity is a property of organisms, so the variety of ecosystems is merely the setting in which biodiversity is found rather than a level of biodiversity itself.
items.why: Earlier definitions of biodiversity mention only organisms and species, and ecosystems are taught as habitats that contain biodiversity, so students treat ecosystem variety as background rather than as something to be measured. Biodiversity is the variety of life at every level, including ecosystem diversity. A region that loses a mangrove or a wetland has lost biodiversity even if every species in it survives elsewhere, because a distinct combination of community and environment has gone.
items.specStatementText: Biodiversity is variety at three levels
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a large or stable population mean that diversity is high?
items.correct: No. Diversity depends on variety, not numbers: a large population can have very low genetic diversity, and a community with many individuals can be dominated by one species.
items.misconception: Diversity is judged by the number of individuals: a large or stable population must be genetically diverse, and a community with more individuals is more diverse.
items.why: Abundance is the quantity that is easiest to observe and count, and population size is the usual measure of whether a species is doing well, so students carry it across to diversity, which is a measure of variety rather than of amount. Genetic diversity is the variety of alleles, not the number of animals: cheetah populations can be stable yet genetically almost uniform. Species diversity depends on richness and evenness, so a community in which one species has become extremely abundant has lower diversity, not higher.
items.specStatementText: Biodiversity is variety at three levels
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Have most of the species on Earth been discovered and named?
items.correct: No. Around two million species have been described, but estimates of the total are several times higher, so many more species remain to be discovered.
items.misconception: Almost every species alive today has already been discovered, named and described, so published species counts are close to the true total.
items.why: Textbooks, field guides and museum displays present classification as finished, and most of the species students meet are large, familiar and long described, so the unnamed majority of insects, fungi and microorganisms is invisible to them. Millions of species have been discovered, named and described, but there are many more species to be discovered. Estimates of the total number of species on Earth are several times the number described, and new species are named every year.
items.specStatementText: More species now than ever, and most are still undescribed
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Were there more species alive in the past, for example in the age of the dinosaurs, than today?
items.correct: No. Evidence from fossils suggests that more species are alive on Earth today than at any time in the past.
items.misconception: Biodiversity has been falling through geological time, because each mass extinction removed species that were never replaced, so the past held more species than the present.
items.why: Students hear far more about extinctions, especially the loss of the dinosaurs, than about diversification, and the word 'crisis' suggests a long decline, so they picture species numbers as having fallen ever since the distant past. The fossil record shows biodiversity recovering and rising after each mass extinction, and the overall trend is upward: there are more species alive today than at any time in the past. The current crisis is the rate at which this diversity is now being lost, not a continuation of a long decline.
items.specStatementText: More species now than ever, and most are still undescribed
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are marine species protected from extinction by the size of the oceans?
items.correct: No. The Caribbean monk seal was hunted to extinction; marine species that gather at coasts to breed, or that are targeted commercially, are as vulnerable as terrestrial ones.
items.misconception: The oceans are so vast that human activity cannot remove a marine species entirely, so extinctions are essentially a problem for land animals.
items.why: Students picture the open ocean as remote and unreachable, and most extinctions they learn about are of land animals and birds, so marine species seem to have somewhere to hide. Marine species depend on particular habitats and often breed at a few accessible sites. Caribbean monk seals were killed on their beaches for blubber oil from the 1490s, their prey were depleted by fishing and their colonies disturbed; the last confirmed sighting was in 1952 and the species was declared extinct in 2008.
items.specStatementText: Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do only direct killing and hunting count as human causes of a species' extinction?
items.correct: No. Indirect anthropogenic pressures, such as loss of habitat, depletion of prey by fishing and disturbance of breeding sites, are also causes of anthropogenic extinction.
items.misconception: A species is driven extinct by people only when they kill it directly; if it dies out because its habitat or food supply changed, that is a natural cause.
items.why: The extinction stories students first meet, such as the dodo, are told as tales of hunting, and 'anthropogenic' is read as 'done on purpose', so indirect effects are filed as nature rather than as human causes. Anthropogenic causes include everything that human activity brings about, directly or indirectly. The moa lost forest to burning as well as birds to hunting; the monk seal lost prey to fishing and breeding beaches to settlement; the passenger pigeon lost its nesting forests to clearance as well as birds to market hunters.
items.specStatementText: Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a very abundant species be driven to extinction?
items.correct: Yes. The passenger pigeon numbered in the billions in the early 1800s and was extinct by 1914; moa were abundant when settlers arrived.
items.misconception: Only rare species are at risk of extinction; a species with a huge population is safe, because people could not remove so many individuals.
items.why: Extinction is pictured as the death of the last few individuals of a rare species, and conservation attention goes to rare species, so abundance is taken as a guarantee of safety. What matters is whether removal exceeds replacement. Commercial hunting of passenger pigeons at their huge nesting colonies, with clearance of the forests they needed, reduced billions of birds to none within a century. Abundance delays extinction but does not prevent it.
items.specStatementText: Humans are causing the sixth mass extinction
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a claim about biodiversity become verifiable evidence once it has been published somewhere?
items.correct: Not simply by publication. Verifiable evidence usually comes from a peer-reviewed source that describes its methodology so that the work can be checked.
items.misconception: Anything that has been published, on a website, in a news report or in a campaign document, counts as evidence that can be cited for a biodiversity crisis.
items.why: In everyday use 'published' means made public, and students are taught to cite sources without being taught the difference between a source and a peer-reviewed one whose methods can be examined. To be verifiable, evidence usually has to come from a published source which has been peer-reviewed and allows the methodology to be checked. Reports from IPBES draw on such sources; a website total or a news headline does not by itself let anyone check how the figures were obtained (NOS).
items.specStatementText: Showing the crisis needs repeated, verifiable surveys
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is ex situ conservation in zoos, botanic gardens and seed banks enough on its own to save a species?
items.correct: No. No single approach is sufficient; ex situ collections hold few individuals and limited genetic diversity, and do not conserve the habitat or the species' ecological role.
items.misconception: Once a species is held in a zoo, botanic garden or seed bank it is safe, so protecting its natural habitat is no longer essential.
items.why: Zoos and seed banks publicize themselves as arks, and the Svalbard vault is reported as a 'doomsday' store, so students take ex situ storage as a complete insurance policy. Ex situ conservation protects individuals and germ plasm and allows captive breeding, but captive populations are small, may lose genetic diversity and natural behaviours, and a species without a habitat has nowhere to return to. In situ conservation, reserve management, rewilding and reclamation are needed alongside it.
items.specStatementText: No single conservation method is enough
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes a species evolutionarily distinct?
items.correct: Having few or no close living relatives, so that it represents a long branch of the phylogenetic tree shared with no other species.
items.misconception: An evolutionarily distinct species is an old, 'primitive' species that has survived unchanged from the distant past, so distinctiveness means being ancient.
items.why: Popular phrases like 'living fossil' and 'ancient lineage' are used for EDGE species, so students equate distinctiveness with age or lack of change rather than with how many living relatives a species has. Every living species has been evolving for the same length of time. Evolutionary distinctiveness measures how much of that history is unique to the species: the aye-aye is distinct because it is the only living member of its family, not because it is older than other lemurs.
items.specStatementText: EDGE prioritizes species that are distinct and endangered
